analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to offer basic health coverage to workers and families and expands Medicaid for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and received a hearing in June 1992, but was never voted on and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nearly every employer to offer workers and their families a certified basic health plan covering hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, preventive care for children, and cancer screening, with caps on deductibles and out-of-pocket costs and no denial for preexisting conditions. People without employer coverage and incomes up to 240% of the poverty line would have become eligible for Medicaid, and uninsured people aged 55 to 64 could buy into Medicare at full cost. Small employers would get a 50% tax credit for health costs, insurers in the small-employer market would face guaranteed-issue and guaranteed-renewal rules, and employers or insurers that failed to comply would owe federal excise taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers that did not previously offer insurance, their families, uninsured people up to 240% of the poverty line who would gain Medicaid coverage, uninsured 55-to-64-year-olds who could buy into Medicare, self-employed people gaining a full health insurance deduction, and low-income workers whose health insurance tax credit would double.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer must offer each eligible employee (working at least 25 hours weekly) a certified plan covering Medicare-level benefits plus prescription drugs, well-child care, cancer screening, immunizations, family planning, and children's dental and vision care, and the offer must include the employee's whole family [S2][S3].

Plans cannot deny or limit basic coverage based on health status, medical history, or insurability, and employee premiums are capped at 20% of the plan's actuarial cost (30% for family coverage), with limits on deductibles, copayments, and total out-of-pocket spending [S3].

Medicaid is extended to people not covered by employer plans or Medicare with income up to 240% of the poverty line, with cost-sharing on a sliding scale and a 5-percentage-point increase in federal payments to states that enroll them in coordinated care plans [S2][S3].

Small employers (fewer than 100 employees) receive a refundable credit worth 50% of their health care costs, the low-income health insurance credit doubles to 12%, and self-employed people get a permanent full deduction for health insurance costs [S2][S3].

Insurers issuing plans to small employers must guarantee eligibility, availability, and renewability, with limits on experience rating; insurers violating the small-employer standards owe an excise tax of 25% of gross premiums, and employers that fail to offer coverage owe $50 per employee per day [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that do not currently offer coverage would bear the cost of providing plans (or the $50-per-day excise tax for failing to), and employees would still pay up to 20-30% of premiums plus capped deductibles and copays. Insurers in the small-employer market would face guaranteed-issue, rating limits, and a 25%-of-premiums excise tax for violations. Federal and state governments would fund the Medicaid expansion and small-employer credits, and workers earning above 100% of poverty in the new Medicaid group would pay sliding-scale premiums and cost-sharing.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face substantial new costs: a mandate to offer certified plans to all employees working 25 or more hours weekly, backed by a $50-per-employee-per-day excise tax for noncompliance, and large employers would be barred from trimming existing extra benefits for two years [S3].

The bill would preempt state laws that require additional benefits, stricter coverage rules, or tougher regulation of managed care and utilization review, preventing states from imposing stronger protections than the federal floor [S3].

Coverage would remain tied to employment and to premiums and cost-sharing paid by workers: employees could still owe up to 20-30% of the actuarial premium, deductibles up to $400 individual/$800 family, and out-of-pocket costs up to $5,000, and the new Medicaid population above 100% of poverty would face sliding-scale premiums and cost sharing [S3].
The Medicaid expansion excludes long-term care services, and people aged 55-64 could buy into Medicare only by paying premiums equal to full actuarial cost, which would be unaffordable for many [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have brought coverage to millions who had none, with real consumer protections (guaranteed issue, premium and out-of-pocket caps, no preexisting-condition exclusions) and help for small employers paying the added cost. The trade-offs were real: a broad employer mandate with tax penalties, continued employee cost-sharing that remains sizable, the exclusion of long-term care from the Medicaid expansion, and federal preemption that overrides stricter state protections, particularly for managed care plans. It was an employer-based, insurer-mediated approach rather than a government plan, so its success would have depended on private plans and state certification working as designed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to its Finance Committee, which held one hearing in June 1992, but the committee never voted to report it and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Packwood introduced the bill on November 26, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
The Finance Committee held hearings on June 9, 1992, but took no further action; the bill was never reported to the Senate and died at the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers avoided a new coverage mandate and the accompanying excise taxes, while the uninsured workers and families the bill would have covered remained without coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; the uninsured stayed uncovered

for.name: Sen. Bob Packwood
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Comprehensive Health Insurance Plan of 1991, a Republican-sponsored proposal for near-universal coverage through employer mandates and Medicaid expansion [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on June 9, 1992 but never marked up or reported the bill to the Senate floor, and it died at the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and it had no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill makes private insurance the mandatory channel for covering workers: every employer must offer a certified plan, and Medicaid can pay premiums for private or coordinated care plans. Insurers gain a large guaranteed market, but they also face guaranteed-issue and guaranteed-renewal rules in the small-employer market, rating limits, and an excise tax of 25% of premiums for violating the standards [S2][S3].

Coordinated care plans get a preferred role, states get a 5-percentage-point boost in federal Medicaid payments for enrolling people in them, and federal law preempts state restrictions on managed care networks, financial incentives, and utilization review [S3]. The same preemption would override state consumer protections on utilization review, cutting against patients.

Employers must offer certified plans or pay a $50-per-employee-per-day excise tax, but small employers get a refundable credit covering 50% of their health care costs and self-employed people get a permanent full deduction, offsetting much of the burden for smaller firms [S2][S3].
